items.title: $5 Million Paid, One Federal Lawsuit: Inside the Justice Department's Challenge to Evanston's Reparations Program
items.body:
## A First-of-Its-Kind Program Faces Its Biggest Test

In 2019, the Evanston, Illinois City Council did something no U.S. municipality had done before: it voted to fund a local reparations program for Black residents harmed by decades of housing discrimination and redlining. Seven years later, that program is at the center of a federal legal battle that could shape whether any American city can run a race-based reparations effort at all.

The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to intervene in a lawsuit against the city, arguing that Evanston's program amounts to unconstitutional racial discrimination. The case is being watched closely far beyond Illinois, since Evanston's program has long served as a model — and a test case — for reparations advocates across the country.

## How Evanston's Program Works

Evanston's "Restorative Housing Program" grew out of a 2019 City Council decision to dedicate the first $10 million collected from the city's 3% cannabis sales tax to reparations efforts. Approved in March 2021, the program offers qualifying Black residents grants of up to $25,000 that can be used toward a down payment, mortgage assistance or home repairs.

To qualify, applicants must have lived in Evanston between 1919 and 1969 — the period during which the city enforced discriminatory housing policies — or be a direct descendant of someone who did. The city has said the program is meant to address documented harm from redlining and other housing discrimination, not to serve as a general benefit based on race alone.

According to court filings, the city has distributed more than $5 million to date, with additional payments planned as funding becomes available. Early rounds of the program provided $25,000 each to dozens of residents, and city officials have said funding constraints — including softer-than-expected cannabis tax revenue — have slowed the pace of payments.

## The Lawsuit That Started It All

The legal challenge began in 2024, when a group of Evanston residents and descendants of former residents who are not Black filed suit in federal court. The case, *Flinn v. City of Evanston*, argues that excluding non-Black applicants from the program violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, which generally bars government programs from distributing benefits based on race.

The city sought to have the case dismissed, arguing the program was a narrowly tailored remedy for specific, documented discrimination rather than a broad racial preference. A federal judge rejected that motion in March 2026, allowing the case to proceed — a ruling that opened the door for the Justice Department's involvement.

## Why the DOJ Stepped In

Shortly after the dismissal was denied, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division opened its own investigation into the Evanston program under the Equal Protection Clause and the federal Fair Housing Act. The department has said the city declined to cooperate with that inquiry, which prompted federal attorneys to seek to formally intervene in the private lawsuit rather than pursue a separate case.

In its filings, the DOJ contends the government has what it calls an "unconditional right" to intervene in cases alleging the denial of equal protection based on race, and argues Evanston's program distributes cash and housing assistance "solely" on the basis of an applicant's race, rather than on individualized proof of harm. The department's proposed complaint asks the court to find the program unlawful under both the Constitution and federal fair-housing law.

Evanston officials and reparations advocates have pushed back, arguing the program is a targeted remedy grounded in a documented history of the city's own discriminatory housing practices between 1919 and 1969 — not an open-ended racial preference. The city's Reparations Committee has said it remains committed to the program while the litigation continues, and some members have framed the case as a test of whether any local government can ever attempt to repair historical harm through direct, race-conscious remedies.

## Why This Case Matters Beyond Evanston

Evanston's program has been widely cited as a national blueprint since its launch, and other cities and states have looked to it while considering their own reparations proposals. Legal observers note that a ruling against Evanston could make it significantly harder for other municipalities to design similar programs, while a ruling in the city's favor could bolster the legal footing for reparations efforts elsewhere.

The case is still in its early stages in federal district court in Illinois, and a ruling on the merits is not expected imminently. Both the underlying *Flinn* lawsuit and the Justice Department's intervention will need to work through further briefing and, potentially, appeals — meaning the ultimate fate of Evanston's program, and its implications for reparations policy nationwide, likely remain months or years away from resolution.
